Furthermore, when the population-mileage formula was originally devised, the impact on cities in the 500,000 and up class was considered negligible:
Of the 5 municipalities with populations of 1,000,000 or more, Detroit is the only one the commercial zone of which has not already been determined and, as above indicated, individual consideration as to it will be provided for. Of the 9 having populations of 500,000 to 1,000,000, 3 have already had their commercial zones determined, and individual consideration has been requested with respect to 3 others. It thus appears that our findings herein will apply to no municipality having a population in excess of 1,000,000, and, to only 3 having populations in excess of 500,000. (Emphasis added) Commercial Zones, 46 M.C.C. at 691.
Our policy decision to eliminate existing individual descriptions of specific commercial zones, which are in many cases confusing, and the quantum leap in the number of cities in the 100,000 and above category renders it necessary to make some adjustment in the present formula.
QUANTIFICATION & METHOD OF EXPANSION:
Certain parties question the advisability of attempting to define commercial zone limits by utilization of a general rule. They assert that only by considering the peculiar characteristics of each municipality on a case-by-case basis can truly accurate bounds be described. Certainly, the cause of exactness would be enhanced by an ad hoc approach to the determination of commercial zone limits. Significant problems are perceived, however, with such an approach. A commercial zone exists about every municipality, and an individual determination for each city, or limited to major cities only, would require a great deal of time
